name: 10-control
description: The surface: eight switches, encoders and faders, each pointed at any control on the device, and the one place external control arrives.

steps.title: Control
steps.caption: Control. One surface, pointed anywhere.

This is the Control module, and it is not an effect or a driver. It is a surface: eight switches, eight encoders and eight faders, and each one can be pointed at any control on this device, and sixty four pads for presets.

Three are wired by hand, because a device with nothing wired is no use, and the rest follow the effect you enabled last. Switch one is the master on and off: the lights stop, and nothing else in the tree changed.
And back on again.
The faders sit right under the encoders, so the whole desk reads at a glance.
Fader one is the brightness, and it is pointed at Drivers dot brightness. Pulling it down here is the same as pulling it down on the Drivers card.
Back up. Every one of these applies on the next frame, like everything else.
And encoder one is a knob: scroll it, and it steps through the palettes. Switch, fader, encoder: on and off, a value, and a choice from a list.
Any slot can be pinned to anything. The link button turns the card into assign mode, and then every control here is a question: what should this one drive?
So press it, and the surface is ready to be wired.
Click the control you want to assign, and it asks where to point it: every module on the device, and every control inside the one you pick.
The effect, say.
and the control on it: the pulse rate.
And assign. Fader two is pinned to the pulse rate now, and it stays there whatever effect comes next.
Done assigning, and the card is a surface again.
And there it goes: the pulse speeds up under the fader. Which is the point: you build the surface you want, rather than the one someone shipped.
Now the part that makes this more than a page of sliders. The surface is where external control arrives, and the services are how it gets in.
O S C is the clearest example: the protocol lighting desks and touch surfaces speak. It is off until you turn it on, because the port takes writes without a password.
Listening now, on port nine thousand. An address like slash m m slash fader slash one reaches that fader directly.

steps.name: osc
steps.caption: So here is a message sent from the command line, the way a desk or a phone app would send it: fader two, a quarter of the way up.
Back to the surface, to see what that did.
There it is: fader two moved on its own, and the effect slowed with it, because that fader is pointed at the pulse rate.

steps.name: osc2
steps.caption: And back up, fast again. The surface is synced either way, whoever moved it.
O S C is one way in. Because these are services, the others work the same: Home Assistant over M Q T T, a MIDI desk, a game pad, a wired switch on a pin, a pedal, an analog dial.
Under the faders is the preset pad, and a preset is a whole look saved onto one of them.
So: a look worth keeping. Bouncing balls.
Back to the surface, where the pads are.
Click an empty pad, and it offers to save what is running right now, and asks which part to keep: the effects, by default.
Give it a name.
Saved: that pad now holds the effects, the whole look.
Now a different look entirely: ripples, which is nothing like bouncing balls.
Back to the pads.
The next empty pad.
Name this one too.
Saved. Two looks now, one on each pad.
Press the first, and the bouncing balls come back, exactly as they were saved.
Press the second, and it is ripples again. Which is what a pad is for: a show is a row of these, one press apart.

And what arrives is always the same eight switches, encoders and faders, and the same sixty four pads. So a game pad, a Mackie desk such as the QCon or the X Touch, and an Akai APC forty mark two are already services, and whatever comes next is one more, not a rewrite.
A preset is a state document, so it shares. The Gallery under the pads holds the presets and scripts other people published, and installs one with a click.
